name: Chichibu-sugi (秩父杉), the Cedar of Takachiho Shrine

location.address: 高千穂神社, 宮崎県西臼杵郡高千穂町三田井1037 (Takachiho Shrine, Takachiho)

access: Free, inside the Takachiho Shrine precinct, open to walk up to; fenced at the foot, so viewed from a few metres away. Nothing booked or paid for the tree.
transport: Takachiho is reached by bus only (no railway): Takachiho Bus Centre (Nobeoka or Kumamoto buses) to the shrine is about 15 minutes' walk, or a few minutes by taxi.

photo_hint.own: sighting 8bfeb681-540d-4b78-8df5-06a95191adb2 (Hidde, 2026-09-28, shows the tree, the Miyazaki 100 Giant Trees sign and the planting-legend sign; approved by him, use uncredited)
photo_hint.commons_alt: File:高千穂神社の大杉 - panoramio.jpg, CC BY-SA 3.0, sk01, 2014-05-22, geotag 32.706308,131.30237

verify_notes:
- Sign in front of the tree (read in Hidde's photograph): みやざきの巨樹百選, 樹木名 スギ, 樹齢 800年, 幹周 715 cm, 樹高 55 m, 所有者 神社, 平成4年3月認定 (as legible, Miyazaki prefecture). Second sign: planted about 800 years ago by Hatakeyama Shigetada as Minamoto no Yoritomo's envoy.
- Matches nishiusuki-shinrin.jp (西臼杵広域森林組合, 銘木紹介): 800 years, 55 m, 715 cm. Town tourism page: 樹齢約800年, planted by 畠山重忠.
- Designation: ja.wikipedia says 高千穂町指定天然記念物, 1969-03-19; hitozato-kyoboku.com gives the same.
- CONFLICT on girth: the national Environment Agency giant-tree survey gives 9.0 m, ja.wikipedia says 'max girth 9 m'; the shrine sign gives 7.15 m and the hitozato site (7.2 m) says 'it is not that thick', taking the sign's figure. Use 715 and say the older survey recorded 9 m. Height 55 m is from the Environment Agency survey and the sign.
- Age basis: the shrine and town board's sign plus legend (Hatakeyama Shigetada, c.1185-1190, Bunji era). Legend of planting, not a dendrochronological date; keep it as 'about 800 years, by the shrine's account'. Name Chichibu comes from Shigetada's home Chichibu (Saitama).
- Pin: OSM node 7073933907 (natural_monument, circumference 7, height 55, name 秩父杉) is 4 m from Hidde's GPS fix 32.7063083,131.3022955 and 5 m from the Commons geotag: three independent fixes agree, so confirmed. Coordinates given are the OSM node.
- Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist observation 2025-09-04 at the spot; Hidde photographed it standing 2026-09-28, with the sign.
- How to find it: it stands to the right of the path through the precinct near the Kagura-den, a single immense unbranched trunk with a fenced foot, a wooden pair of signs and a white post reading 秩父杉; the nearby Meoto-sugi is ~35 m away at the honden.

name: Meoto-sugi (夫婦杉), the Wedded Cedars of Takachiho Shrine

location.address: 高千穂神社 拝殿前, 宮崎県西臼杵郡高千穂町三田井1037 (in front of the haiden, Takachiho Shrine)

access: Free, inside the Takachiho Shrine precinct, by the haiden and honden; fenced, with ema racks at the fence. Shrine hours daily; no booking.
transport: Takachiho is reached by bus only (no railway): Takachiho Bus Centre to the shrine is about 15 minutes' walk, or a few minutes by taxi.

photo_hint.own: sighting b9a2d2df-77ba-4240-8c90-63ca0a83b1c9 (Hidde, 2026-09-28; two trunks joined at the base, shimenawa, ema fence, honden behind; approved, uncredited)

verify_notes:

- AGE CONFLICT, flagged: ANA travel and another travel page say about 800 years; a separate tourist page says 400 years. No source with a measurement or designation; no girth or height recorded. Deliver as 'several hundred years' (range 400-800) and let the page ask the reader for a girth.

- Recognition: two trunks fused at the base behind a shimenawa, a small roofed offering box and ema fence at their foot, in front of the honden's side.

name: The Ogatama of Amano Iwato Shrine (招霊の木)

location.address: 天岩戸神社 西本宮, 宮崎県西臼杵郡高千穂町岩戸1073-1 (West Shrine, Amano Iwato Shrine)

access: Free; the shrine precinct is open 8:30 to 16:30 all year (town tourism page). The tree stands inside the fence beside the West Shrine's building, so it is viewed over the fence. Viewing the sacred cave across the river is a separate booked visit and not needed for the tree.
transport: About 6 km east of Takachiho town centre; local bus or taxi from Takachiho Bus Centre (timetable not verified).

verify_notes:

- Species: ogatama-no-ki, which the shrine and town name directly; Latin name is the standard one for the common name, not stated on those pages.

A reader will have to tell us whether it is old; the case for the page is the myth and the tree itself (a multi-stemmed trunk bound with shimenawa) rather than a record size.

name: Ginkgo of Shimono Hachiman Shrine (下野八幡大神社のイチョウ)

location.address: 下野八幡大神社, 宮崎県西臼杵郡高千穂町下野 (Shimono Hachiman Shrine, Takachiho)

access: Free, shrine precinct, open to walk into; no booking or entry fee found. Access beyond the approach not confirmed by a source.
transport: Takachiho is reached by bus only (no railway). Shimono is about 5 km north-east of the centre (roughly 12 minutes by taxi from Takachiho Bus Centre); the local bus is infrequent, so check the timetable or take a taxi.
story:
Japan made this ginkgo a national natural monument in June 1951, and the measurements explain why: 9.20 metres round at chest height and 36.4 metres tall, which is a very large ginkgo by any standard. The Agency for Cultural Affairs records it as a female tree, so in autumn it drops its fruit on the shrine ground, the soft, pungent seeds every Japanese ginkgo-watcher knows by smell before sight.

It stands on the left of the approach to Shimono Hachiman Shrine, about five kilometres north-east of Takachiho's centre. The town puts its age at about 800 years and counts it among Miyazaki Prefecture's hundred giant trees. The town gives no method for the figure, so read it as a local estimate rather than a ring count, somewhere in the range of six to nine centuries.

On the other side of the approach stands a second national monument, a zelkova designated the same day, so the shrine is guarded on both flanks.

Getting here takes some planning. Takachiho has no railway, the local bus to Shimono runs rarely, and a taxi from the bus centre takes about twelve minutes. Late November is the time: the ginkgo turns gold and the ground beneath it follows.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the giant ginkgo on the left of the approach to Shimono Hachiman Shrine, 9.20 metres round and 36.4 metres tall; the zelkova on the right, against the shrine building, is the other monument.

best_time.label: late November, when the ginkgo turns gold over the shrine approach

name: Zelkova of Shimono Hachiman Shrine (下野八幡大神社のケヤキ)

location.address: 下野八幡大神社, 宮崎県西臼杵郡高千穂町下野 (Shimono Hachiman Shrine, Takachiho)

access: Free, shrine precinct, open to walk into; no booking or entry fee found. Access beyond the approach not confirmed by a source.
transport: Takachiho is reached by bus only (no railway). Shimono is about 5 km north-east of the centre (roughly 12 minutes by taxi from Takachiho Bus Centre); the local bus is infrequent, so check the timetable or take a taxi.
story:
The crown of this zelkova spreads 26 metres one way and 33 the other, nearly as wide as the tree is tall. The Agency for Cultural Affairs, which has listed it as a national natural monument since June 1951, gives the rest of the measurements: 34.7 metres tall and 8 metres round at chest height.

There is a bigger number in the same record, and it needs care. Measured round the roots, the tree comes to 20.80 metres. That is the buttressed mass of the base where it meets the ground, not the trunk, and the gap between 8 and 20.80 tells you how far the foot of this tree spreads before it rises.

It stands on the right of the approach to Shimono Hachiman Shrine, about five kilometres north-east of central Takachiho, close against the shrine building. Across the approach is the shrine's great ginkgo, designated on the same day in 1951, so a single visit takes in two national monuments a few steps apart.

Nobody has published an age for it. The national record gives none, and a girth alone is not enough to name one honestly. If you know the shrine's own account of when this tree was planted, or how old the shrine considers it, tell us.

Go in November. Zelkovas turn russet and orange in late autumn, and so does the ginkgo opposite, in gold, which makes it the month the two trees peak together.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the huge zelkova close against the shrine building on the right of the approach, its base spread wide in buttresses; the giant ginkgo stands across the approach on the left.

best_time.label: November, when the zelkova turns russet beside the gold ginkgo
